title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
tagline: From Dobereiner's triads to Moseley's law — and the periodic trends that let you predict an element's behaviour from its position.

overview.intro: Sorting the elements is not bookkeeping: a successful classification predicts properties before they are measured. This unit follows the genesis of periodic classification from Dobereiner's triads and Newlands' octaves through Mendeleev's table — which left gaps and predicted gallium, scandium and germanium — to Moseley's modern periodic law based on atomic number. You will learn how the table is read today, how the s-, p-, d- and f-blocks arise from electronic configuration, and how atomic radius, ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity and metallic character vary across a period and down a group, with the anomalies explained by shielding and nuclear charge.

learningOutcomes: Trace the development of periodic classification and explain how Mendeleev's law differed from the modern periodic law.
Derive the block, group and period of an element from its electronic configuration, and write the name of any element from its atomic number.
Predict and explain the trends in atomic and ionic radii, ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity and metallic character.
Account for the anomalies in the periodic trends, including the inert-pair effect and the second-period inversions.

blocks.text: Before a periodic table could exist, elements had to be compared on a common basis. Dobereiner noticed in 1829 that in groups of three similar elements — chlorine, bromine and iodine; calcium, strontium and barium; lithium, sodium and potassium — the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the average of the other two. These triads gave partial success but could not classify all known elements. Newlands, arranging the fifty-six known elements in order of increasing atomic mass in 1865, found that every eighth element resembled the first, like the musical octaves he played on the violin. His law of octaves worked only up to calcium and forced dissimilar elements into the same family, so it was ridiculed and abandoned.

Mendeleev's contribution in 1869 was to organise the elements by atomic mass while insisting on chemical similarity: he arranged them in order of increasing atomic mass and placed elements with similar properties in the same vertical group, giving the law that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic mass. Two features made his table scientific rather than cosmetic. He left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties — eka-boron, eka-aluminium and eka-silicon became scandium, gallium and germanium, whose discovered properties matched his predictions closely. And he reversed the expected order of certain pairs, such as tellurium and iodine, when chemical evidence demanded it. The table nevertheless contained anomalies: the tellurium-iodine inversion, the inconsistent positions of the noble gases (not yet discovered) and the placement of cobalt before nickel, all of which were resolved when the true ordering variable was found.

That variable was atomic number. In 1913 Moseley measured the frequencies of the characteristic X-rays emitted by different metals and found that the square root of the frequency is a linear function of the atomic number: √ν = a(Z − b). Atomic number, not atomic mass, is therefore the fundamental property. The modern periodic law states that the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number. With this, the inversions disappear naturally: tellurium (Z = 52) precedes iodine (Z = 53), cobalt (Z = 27) precedes nickel (Z = 28), and the noble gases fall into their own group as increasing atomic number rather than increasing mass demands.

learn.title: The modern periodic table and nomenclature

blocks.text: The modern periodic law — properties are a periodic function of atomic number — gives the long form of the periodic table arranged in order of increasing atomic number. There are seven horizontal periods, numbered 1 to 7, where the period number equals the highest principal quantum number of the elements it contains: period 1 (hydrogen and helium) has n = 1, period 2 and 3 have n = 2 and n = 3 with eight elements each, period 4 and 5 have eighteen elements, and periods 6 and 7 contain thirty-two with the fourteen lanthanoids and actinoids shown separately below to keep the table workable. The vertical columns are groups; the present numbering runs 1 to 18, with the older CAS labels I A to VII A and I B to VII B still met in older books. Elements are placed so that each group shares an outer-shell configuration: group 1 has ns¹, group 2 ns², groups 13-18 ns²np¹-ns²np⁶, and the transition series fill the (n−1)d subshell.

The four blocks follow from which subshell is being filled. The s-block comprises groups 1 and 2 plus helium: these metals are soft, have low melting points, form mainly ionic compounds and have one or two valence electrons. The p-block spans groups 13 to 18 and contains metals, metalloids and non-metals together with the noble gases. The d-block elements are the transition elements of groups 3 to 10, in which the (n−1)d subshell fills, and they show variable oxidation states, colour and catalytic behaviour. The f-block, the lanthanoids and actinoids placed below the table, fills the 4f and 5f subshells and shows an almost uniform +3 oxidation state. Metalloids such as boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony and tellurium lie along the zig-zag line separating metals from non-metals and form the semiconductors on which modern electronics depends.

For elements with atomic number above 100, IUPAC naming uses the roots nil (0), un (1), bi (2), tri (3), quad (4), pent (5), hex (6), sept (7), oct (8) and enn (9), assembled in order of the digits and given the suffix -ium: element 104 is unnilquadium, later named rutherfordium, and element 118, written ununoctium, was named oganesson in 2016. The system lets any new element be named unambiguously before its chemistry is fully known.

items: Group 1 (alkali metals) and group 2 (alkaline earth metals) are s-block; groups 13-18 are p-block; groups 3-10 are d-block transition elements.

The lanthanoids (4f filling) and actinoids (5f filling) are placed below the table to keep it to 18 columns.
Zig-zag line separates metals (left) from non-metals (right), with metalloids along the line.

blocks.text: Atomic radius decreases across a period from left to right and increases down a group. Across a period the nuclear charge increases while new electrons enter the same shell, so the extra charge pulls the shell inwards; down a group each element adds a whole shell, which outweighs the increase in nuclear charge. The same reasoning gives ionic radii: a cation is smaller than its parent atom because it has lost a shell or lost electron-electron repulsion, while an anion is larger because the same nuclear charge now holds more electrons. Isoelectronic species — N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺ all with ten electrons — are compared by nuclear charge: the greater the atomic number, the smaller the ion, so Al³⁺ < Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < O²⁻ < N³⁻.

Ionisation enthalpy is the energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom; the first ionisation enthalpy ΔᵢH₁ is followed by second and third values that are always larger because a positive ion holds its electrons more tightly. Ionisation enthalpy increases across a period and decreases down a group, because the same factors that shrink the atom also bind the electron more strongly. The trend is not smooth: across period 2 there is a dip at beryllium (the 2s electron is removed rather than a higher-energy 2p electron) and again at nitrogen (the 2p³ half-filled subshell gains exchange stability), and across period 3 the same dips appear at magnesium and phosphorus. The noble gases, with filled shells, have the highest ionisation enthalpies of their periods.

Electron gain enthalpy is the energy released when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom; a more negative value means a stronger tendency to gain an electron. It becomes more negative across a period and less negative down a group. Chlorine has a more negative electron gain enthalpy than fluorine, because the incoming electron in the tiny fluorine atom enters a compact 2p subshell and suffers strong electron-electron repulsion. Electron gain enthalpies of the noble gases are close to zero, and nitrogen's is nearly zero because a fifth electron would have to enter a paired 2p orbital. Electronegativity — the ability of an atom to attract the shared pair in a bond — follows the same trend and is highest for fluorine (4.0 on the Pauling scale); it rises across a period and falls down a group, and elements above 2.0 are classed as non-metals.

learn.title: Anomalies: inert pair effect and the d-block contraction

blocks.text: Two anomalies are worth learning explicitly because they explain departures from the plain trends. The inert pair effect is the reluctance of the outermost s-electrons to participate in bonding in the heavier elements of groups 13 to 15. In gallium the +3 and +1 states are close in energy, but by thallium the 6s² pair is stabilised by poor shielding by the 4f electrons and the +1 state is more stable; similarly lead shows +2 in preference to +4 and bismuth prefers +3 to +5. The effect becomes more pronounced down the group, so the lower oxidation state of the heavier element is the more stable even though the group maximum is unchanged.

items.text: Arrange in increasing atomic radius: K, Mg, Ca and Na, and explain.
items.note: Atomic radius increases down a group and decreases across a period. Na and K are in group 1 with K below Na, so K > Na. Mg and Ca are in group 2 with Ca below Mg, so Ca > Mg. Across period 3, Na > Mg, and across period 4, K > Ca. Overall: Mg < Ca < Na < K (Mg 160 pm, Ca 197 pm, Na 186 pm, K 243 pm).

items.text: Why is the first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen greater than that of oxygen?
items.note: Nitrogen is 1s² 2s² 2p³, a exactly half-filled p subshell whose exchange energy makes it unusually stable, while oxygen is 1s² 2s² 2p⁴, where one 2p orbital holds a pair whose repulsion makes an electron easier to remove. Hence ΔᵢH₁(N) = 1402 kJ mol⁻¹ exceeds ΔᵢH₁(O) = 1314 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.text: Explain why the electron gain enthalpy of chlorine is more negative than that of fluorine.
items.note: Both add an electron to a p subshell, but in fluorine the incoming electron enters the compact 2p subshell close to the nucleus where the existing electrons repel it strongly; in chlorine the 3p subshell is larger and more diffuse, so the incoming electron is less repelled. Hence Δ egH is −349 kJ mol⁻¹ for Cl and only −328 kJ mol⁻¹ for F.

questions.prompt: The modern periodic law is based on:
questions.explanation: Moseley's experiment showed that the square root of the characteristic X-ray frequency varies linearly with atomic number, so properties are a periodic function of atomic number, not atomic mass.

All four are isoelectronic with ten electrons, so size is decided by nuclear charge: the smallest nuclear charge holds the electrons least tightly. O²⁻ (Z = 8) has the lowest charge of the four, so it is the largest, followed by F⁻ (Z = 9), Na⁺ (Z = 11) and Mg²⁺ (Z = 12).

questions.prompt: The element with electronic configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³ belongs to:
questions.explanation: The highest principal quantum number is 4, so the element is in period 4, and the valence configuration 4s² 4p³ gives six valence electrons — group 15 (the pnictogens). The element is arsenic, Z = 33.

questions.prompt: Which pair shows the correct order of first ionisation enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Across period 3 ionisation enthalpy generally rises, but two inversions occur: Mg (3s²) is higher than Al (the 3p electron is higher in energy and screens), and P (3p³ half-filled) is higher than S (the fourth 3p electron is paired and repelled). The order Mg > Al > P > S captures both anomalies.

questions.prompt: The number of periods and groups in the long form of the periodic table are __________ and __________.
questions.explanation: The long form has seven horizontal periods and eighteen vertical groups; the period number equals the highest principal quantum number of the elements it contains.

questions.prompt: The IUPAC root used for the digit 4 in the naming of elements with atomic number above 100 is __________.
questions.explanation: The roots are nil (0), un (1), bi (2), tri (3), quad (4), pent (5), hex (6), sept (7), oct (8) and enn (9); element 104 was therefore named unnilquadium before being named rutherfordium.

questions.prompt: Why did Mendeleev's periodic table have to reverse the expected order of tellurium and iodine?
questions.answer: Mendeleev ordered the elements by increasing atomic mass, but tellurium (127.6 u) is heavier than iodine (126.9 u), so mass alone would place iodine first. Tellurium is clearly a group 16 element and iodine a group 17 halogen by chemical similarity, so Mendeleev reversed them to keep the families intact. Moseley's later work resolved the anomaly properly: tellurium has atomic number 52 and iodine 53, so by atomic number the order is correct without any reversal.
questions.explanation: Historical anomaly questions test why the mass-based ordering failed: reversing the pair preserved chemical families, and the later atomic-number basis removed the contradiction entirely.

questions.prompt: Define first ionisation enthalpy and explain why it increases from sodium to chlorine.
questions.answer: First ionisation enthalpy is the energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state. From sodium to chlorine the nuclear charge increases by one at each step while the new electron enters the same third shell, so the effective nuclear attraction on the outer electron grows, the atomic radius shrinks from 186 pm to 99 pm, and more energy is needed to remove the electron — rising from 496 kJ mol⁻¹ for sodium to 1251 kJ mol⁻¹ for chlorine.
questions.explanation: The trend follows from nuclear charge rising while new electrons enter the same shell; quoting the actual values of sodium and chlorine strengthens the answer.

questions.prompt: Describe the inert pair effect and use it to explain the stability of +1 thallium and +2 lead over their higher oxidation states.
questions.answer: The inert pair effect is the reluctance of the outermost ns² electrons to take part in bonding in the heavier elements of groups 13 to 15. Down each group the outer s electrons are held more tightly because the intervening d and f electrons shield the nucleus poorly, so the s pair is stabilised and requires more energy to involve. Thallium (6s²) therefore prefers the +1 state to +3, since promoting one 6s electron costs more energy than the single bond it would form repays; lead (6s²) prefers +2 to +4 for the same reason, and bismuth prefers +3 to +5. The effect is negligible in the second period, so aluminium is comfortably +3 and carbon is +4.
questions.explanation: The inert pair effect must be linked to poor shielding by the intervening d and f electrons, which stabilises the ns2 pair and makes the lower oxidation state of the heavier element the more stable one.

questions.prompt: Compare the first and second ionisation enthalpies of magnesium (ΔᵢH₁ = 738, ΔᵢH₂ = 1451 kJ mol⁻¹) with those of sodium (496 and 4562 kJ mol⁻¹), and explain both the general increase and the enormous jump in the case of sodium.
questions.answer: Both elements show a second ionisation enthalpy far above the first because the second electron must be removed from a species that is already positive, so the same nuclear charge holds fewer electrons more tightly. The general order of magnitude is the same for both. The striking difference is in the ratio: sodium's second value (4562 kJ mol⁻¹) is more than nine times its first, whereas magnesium's is under twice its first. Removing sodium's first electron gives the stable neon configuration, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ — so the second electron must be torn out of a completed noble-gas shell, which is extraordinarily costly. Magnesium's first removal leaves the same neon-like configuration (Mg⁺ is [Ne] 3s¹), and its second removal takes that single 3s electron to reach it, which is difficult but far less so than breaking into a filled shell. The comparison shows that ionisation enthalpy depends not only on charge and size but on whether a stable electronic configuration must be broken into.
questions.explanation: Comparing ratios rather than raw values is what exposes the noble-gas configuration effect; the same reasoning explains why the second ionisation enthalpy of lithium is so large.
